title: Reviewing the alms round
hook: after the alms walk, ask: did desire arise on the way?

segments.voice: Yesterday: the village of Nagaravinda, and your line, who to respect. Whose handling of wanting and anger did you notice? Today, a way to check your own. Day five hundred sixteen.

Sariputta comes out of his solitary sitting one evening in the Bamboo Grove at Rajagaha and goes to the Buddha. The Buddha looks at him and says: Sariputta, your faculties are clear. Your face is pure and bright. What have you been abiding in? Emptiness, venerable sir. Good, the Buddha says. That is the abiding of great people. And then, instead of praising the meditation further, he talks about something ordinary: the morning walk into town to collect food. Today: reviewing the alms round.
screen: `EVENING, THE BAMBOO GROVE.` → `YOUR FACE IS CLEAR AND BRIGHT.` → `NOW: THE MORNING WALK.`

segments.voice: A monk who wants to dwell in emptiness, the Buddha says, should look back like this. On the road I took into the village for alms, in the place where I walked collecting food, on the road I took back: was there any desire, lust, hate, delusion or aversion in my mind toward the things I saw? The things I heard, smelled, tasted, touched, thought? If he finds there was, he should make an effort to let it go. If he finds there wasn't, he can live with that gladness, training day and night. That's it. A walk, remembered honestly. The alms round, pindapata, is a walk monks still make today in Theravada countries, bowl in hand, receiving whatever is given. So it's a good test: sights of food, smells from kitchens, people kind and people not. Then the discourse widens the review into a long checklist. Have I let go of the five strands of sense pleasure? The five hindrances? Have I understood the five heaps? Developed the foundations of mindfulness, the factors of awakening, the eightfold path? Calm and insight? Each time, the same two answers: if not yet, keep making effort; if so, rest in that gladness. The title of the discourse means the purification of almsfood. The idea is that a walk reviewed this way makes the food, and the life it supports, clean. What's striking is the tone. No guilt, no punishment. Just an honest look back at the road, and then the next step. Notice too who it's taught to: Sariputta, whose bright face the Buddha has just praised. Even he is told to check.
screen: `DID DESIRE ARISE ON THE WAY?` · `IF SO, LET IT GO; IF NOT, BE GLAD` · `THE LONG CHECKLIST` · `A WALK REVIEWED, A LIFE MADE CLEAN` · then, large: `REVIEW THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: review your walk home. Or your last trip anywhere: to the store, the office, the kitchen. Close your eyes and replay it slowly. The door. The street or hallway. What you saw. Did wanting rise somewhere? Irritation? A fog? Where was it, exactly? If you find something, just note it and breathe it out. If you find a stretch that was clear, rest there and be glad. The bell holds the time.
Reviewing the alms round. Looking back honestly at the road you walked: if desire arose, let it go; if not, be glad and keep training. Today's word.
Your line: review the road. Tonight, before sleep, walk back through one trip you made today and see what rose on the way. Day five hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: In Theravada countries monks still walk an alms round, bowl in hand, and looking back over one's actions, taught here and in the earlier advice to Rahula (MN 61), is part of monastic and lay training.

fork.setup: you're a monk back from the alms round. reviewing the road, you find there was no lust or aversion on the way. what does MN 151 say to do?
options: live with that gladness, training day and night.
walk the route again to be sure.
tell the other monks about it.
fork.reveal: the text allows gladness: if the road was clear, rest in that joy and keep training.

original.note: Pali pindapata: almsfood, and the alms round that collects it.

trapdoor: what you thought: the alms round is just how monks get lunch.
what it means: in MN 151 it becomes a practice, reviewed afterward for desire, hate and delusion.
what a scholar hears: the title, Pindapataparisuddhi, means purification of almsfood: the review is how a monastic makes the gift that sustains them well used.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 151, Pindapataparisuddhi Sutta (the purification of almsfood)
